_comment: How-to entries for the assistant: what a programmer wants to do, with the registers and the steps. Each one is a short recipe built from the register entries and notes in tia.json, riot.json, formats.json and tv.json (the sources are the same). 'verified': false means a part could not be confirmed from those sources (the routines marked so were not run for this entry). Written for VCSIDE in our own words.

techniques.title: Put a sprite, missile or ball at a given X position
techniques.summary: Two stages: a coarse position from when RESPx is written in the line (steps of 15 pixels with a divide-by-15 loop), then a fine adjustment of -8..+7 pixels with HMxx and one HMOVE.
steps: STA WSYNC first, so the code starts at a known cycle of a line.
Divide the wanted X by 15 with SEC / SBC #15 / BCS loop: one pass is 5 cycles = 15 pixels, so the number of passes sets the coarse position.
Turn the remainder into the fine value for HMxx (high nibble, signed: $70 = 7 pixels left, $00 = none, $80 = 8 pixels right).
STA RESPx at the end of the loop. The object does not move on the current line: it appears from the next one.

When every object is placed: STA WSYNC, then STA HMOVE straight away: it has to be strobed at the start of the line. It also blanks the first 8 pixels of that line (the HMOVE comb), so do it on a line that does not matter, such as one in the vertical blank, or hide the column with a border.
STA HMCLR afterwards, so later HMOVE strobes do not keep moving the objects.
techniques.example:
; A = wanted X (0-159), X register = object: 0 P0, 1 P1, 2 M0, 3 M1, 4 ball
SetX:  sta WSYNC
       sec
.Div:  sbc #15
       bcs .Div
       eor #7
       asl
       asl
       asl
       asl
       sta HMP0,x   ; fine motion (HMP0..HMBL are consecutive)
       sta RESP0,x  ; coarse position (RESP0..RESBL are consecutive)
       rts
techniques.note: The routine is the usual community form and has not been run for this entry: calibrate the constants in an emulator (the exact pixel depends on the cycles spent before RESPx).

techniques.title: Structure of a frame: VSYNC, vertical blank, picture, overscan
techniques.summary: The TIA does not count lines: the program must produce 262 lines every frame on NTSC (3 VSYNC + 37 vertical blank + 192 picture + 30 overscan) and 312 on PAL (3 + 45 + 228 + 36), always the same number.
steps: VSYNC: write 2 to VSYNC, run 3 WSYNC, write 0.
Vertical blank (VBLANK bit 1 set): 37 lines = 2812 CPU cycles on NTSC. Do the game logic here and time it with TIM64T, then wait on INTIM; 43 is a typical start value, adjust it to your code.
Picture: write 0 to VBLANK after a WSYNC, then one WSYNC per line for 192 lines.
Overscan: write 2 to VBLANK, 30 lines = 2280 cycles (a typical TIM64T value is 35), more game logic.
Jump back to VSYNC. Check the line count in the emulator: a frame that is not constant makes the picture roll.
techniques.example:
Frame: lda #2
       sta VSYNC
       sta WSYNC
       sta WSYNC
       sta WSYNC
       lda #0
       sta VSYNC
       lda #43
       sta TIM64T     ; vertical blank, about 37 lines
       ; ... game logic ...
.WaitVB: lda INTIM
       bne .WaitVB
       sta WSYNC
       sta VBLANK     ; A = 0: picture on
       ldx #192
.Line: sta WSYNC
       ; ... draw one line ...
       dex
       bne .Line
       lda #2
       sta VBLANK     ; picture off
       lda #35
       sta TIM64T     ; overscan, about 30 lines
       ; ... more logic ...
.WaitOS: lda INTIM
       bne .WaitOS
       jmp Frame

techniques.title: The picture rolls, flickers or loses sync
techniques.summary: Almost always the number of lines per frame is not constant or not 262 (NTSC) / 312 (PAL), or VSYNC is shorter than 3 lines.
steps: Count the lines your code produces: 3 VSYNC + vertical blank + picture + overscan must add up to 262 on NTSC.
Look for a section that sometimes takes more or fewer lines: a missing WSYNC, a loop that runs a variable number of times, a branch that crosses a page and costs an extra cycle at the wrong moment.
If you time a section with a timer, make sure the code between the write and the wait never takes longer than the timer; a timer that expired early or late shifts the whole frame.
Check with the emulator's scanline counter (Stella reports the detected number of lines) and fix the section that differs.
An indexed store that wraps into the TIA mirrors can write VSYNC by accident: check stray STA abs,X writes.

techniques.title: Read the joystick, the fire button and the console switches
techniques.summary: Joystick directions come from SWCHA (0 = pressed), the fire button from INPT4 and INPT5 (bit 7, 0 = pressed) and the console switches from SWCHB.
steps: The fire button is not in SWCHA: read it from INPT4 (player 0) or INPT5 (player 1), bit 7, 0 = pressed. SWCHA holds only the four directions of each joystick.
SWCHA bits 7-4 are player 0: 7 = right, 6 = left, 5 = down, 4 = up; bits 3-0 are player 1 in the same order. A bit that reads 0 means pressed.
Test one direction with BIT or AND, for example LDA SWCHA then AND #%00100000 and BNE when it is not pressed (down).
INPT4 is the fire button of player 0 and INPT5 of player 1: bit 7 = 0 while pressed. LDA INPT4 then BMI means not pressed.
SWCHB: bit 0 = RESET, bit 1 = SELECT (0 = pressed), bit 3 = colour/B&W, bits 6 and 7 = difficulty of player 0 and 1.
Read them once per frame, in the vertical blank or the overscan, not in the middle of the picture.
techniques.example:
lda INPT4
        bmi NotFire    ; bit 7 = 1: not pressed
        ; fire is pressed
NotFire:
        lda SWCHA
        and #%00100000 ; bit 5 = player 0 down
        bne NotDown    ; 1 = not pressed
        ; down is pressed
NotDown:

techniques.title: Detect that two objects touched
techniques.summary: The TIA latches a bit whenever two objects overlap on any pixel, whatever their colours. Read the collision registers after the picture has been drawn and clear the latches with CXCLR before the next frame.
steps: Draw the frame normally; the latches are set during the picture.

In the overscan or the vertical blank read the register for the pair you care about, bit 7 or bit 6: CXP0FB (player 0 with playfield or ball), CXP1FB, CXM0FB, CXM1FB, CXM0P, CXM1P, CXBLPF, CXPPMM (player with player, missile with missile).
The other bits of those registers are not driven, so test with BIT (N flag = bit 7, V flag = bit 6) or mask with AND #$80 / #$40.
STA CXCLR at the start of the next frame (any write clears all 15 latches); otherwise a collision from a previous frame stays set.
Collisions are pixel overlaps: an object hidden by priority or drawn in the background colour still collides.
techniques.example:
bit CXP0FB
        bmi HitWall    ; bit 7: player 0 touched the playfield
        bvs HitBall    ; bit 6: player 0 touched the ball
        ; ... at the start of the next frame:
        sta CXCLR

techniques.title: Play a tone or a noise
techniques.summary: Each of the two channels has a waveform (AUDCx), a pitch divider (AUDFx) and a volume (AUDVx). Write them once and the sound keeps playing until you change it.
steps: AUDC0 bits 3-0 choose the waveform: 4 and 5 give a high pure tone, 12 and 13 a lower pure tone, 6 and 10 the lowest pure tone, 8 white noise, 0 silence.
AUDF0 bits 4-0 divide the audio clock by AUDF0 + 1: a larger value is a lower note. The audio clock is the colour clock divided by 114 (about 31.4 kHz on NTSC), further divided by the AUDC waveform.
AUDV0 bits 3-0 set the volume 0-15; write 0 to silence the channel.
To play a sequence, change AUDF0 (and AUDV0 for the envelope) once per frame or once per note from your frame loop.
Channel 1 uses AUDC1, AUDF1 and AUDV1 in the same way.
techniques.example:
lda #4
        sta AUDC0      ; pure tone
        lda #15
        sta AUDF0      ; pitch (larger = lower)
        lda #8
        sta AUDV0      ; volume

techniques.title: Choose the background, playfield and sprite colours
techniques.summary: Each colour register holds the hue in the high nibble and the luminance in bits 3-1 of the low nibble.
steps: COLUBK is the background, COLUPF the playfield and ball, COLUP0 player 0 and missile 0, COLUP1 player 1 and missile 1.
Value = hue * 16 + luminance * 2: bits 7-4 hue (0-15), bits 3-1 luminance (0-7), bit 0 ignored.
The hue numbers mean different colours on NTSC, PAL and SECAM (see the TV standards entry). On SECAM only the luminance chooses the colour.
You can change them in the middle of the picture, per line, for gradients: write the register after a WSYNC.
With CTRLPF bit 1 (SCORE) the left half of the playfield uses COLUP0 and the right half COLUP1.

techniques.title: Draw walls and scenery with the playfield
techniques.summary: The playfield is 40 pixels wide in two halves of 20 bits (4 pixels each) taken from PF0, PF1 and PF2; the right half repeats or mirrors the left.
steps: PF0 bits 4-7 give the first 4 bits (bit 4 leftmost), then PF1 bits 7-0, then PF2 bits 0-7: PF1 is shown from its highest bit, PF0 and PF2 from their lowest.
CTRLPF bit 0 = 0 repeats the left half on the right, = 1 mirrors it.
There is no enable bit: write 0 to PF0, PF1 and PF2 to hide the playfield.
To change the pattern line by line, rewrite PF0-PF2 after each WSYNC; to make the halves different, write the registers again in the middle of the line, after the left half has been drawn.
CTRLPF bit 1 (SCORE) colours the left half with COLUP0 and the right with COLUP1; bit 2 draws the playfield in front of the sprites.

techniques.title: Wait a precise time without counting every instruction
techniques.summary: The RIOT timer counts down by itself: load it with TIM1T, TIM8T, TIM64T or T1024T, do other work, and read INTIM to know when it reached zero.
steps: Pick the divider: TIM1T counts every cycle (up to 255), TIM8T every 8 (up to 2040), TIM64T every 64 (up to 16320 = about 214 lines), T1024T every 1024.
Write the start value N: the interval is about N times the divider cycles. A scanline is 76 cycles, so TIM64T is the usual choice for whole sections of a frame.
Do other work, then loop on INTIM until it reads 0 (LDA INTIM / BNE).
After zero the timer keeps counting down from $FF, one per cycle, until you write a new value.
To wait for the end of the current scanline use STA WSYNC instead.
techniques.example:
lda #43
        sta TIM64T
.Wait:  lda INTIM
        bne .Wait

techniques.title: The game is larger than 4 KB: bankswitching
techniques.summary: The CPU sees only 4 KB of cartridge at a time. A bigger ROM is split into 4 KB banks and the program switches between them by touching special addresses (hotspots).
steps: Pick the format by size: F8 = 8 KB (2 banks), F6 = 16 KB (4 banks), F4 = 32 KB (8 banks); 2 KB and 4 KB need no switching.
F8: accessing $1FF8 selects bank 0 and $1FF9 selects bank 1 (a read or a write). F6: $1FF6 to $1FF9 select banks 0-3. F4: $1FF4 to $1FFB select banks 0-7.
The vectors at $FFFA-$FFFF must be valid in every bank, because the bank at power-up is not known.
The code that does the switching should sit at the same addresses in every bank, so execution continues in the new bank on the next instruction.
Set the format in the project (VCSIDE) and in the emulator; the knowledge base has the full list of formats and the extra-RAM variants (SC).

techniques.title: A sprite wider than 8 pixels: the 48-pixel technique
techniques.summary: One player is 8 pixels wide. Two players with three close copies each (NUSIZ = 3) placed side by side cover 48 pixels, and the six graphics bytes of each line are written in turn with the vertical delay registers.
steps: Set NUSIZ0 and NUSIZ1 to 3 (three copies, 16 pixels apart): each player shows its graphics three times on the line.
Place player 0 and player 1 8 pixels apart so their copies interleave into a block of 48 pixels.

Each line needs six different bytes: GRP0 and GRP1 are rewritten in the middle of the line, in fixed cycle windows, with VDELP0 and VDELP1 = 1 so the new value of one player is delayed until the other is written.
The timing is tight (the whole line is spent on the loads), so the kernel is usually written once and reused for score displays and big text.
A narrower and simpler alternative: double or quad width with NUSIZ (5 or 7) for one big 16 or 32 pixel block.
techniques.note: The structure comes from the register descriptions; the exact cycle windows of the six writes were not worked out for this entry. Use a known 48-pixel routine and check it in an emulator.

techniques.title: Do something when the fire button is pressed (once per press)
techniques.summary: Read INPT4 (player 0) or INPT5 (player 1), bit 7 (0 = pressed). To act once per press and not on every frame, keep the previous state in RAM and act only when it changed from released to pressed.
steps: The joystick fire button is not in SWCHA: read INPT4 (player 0) or INPT5 (player 1). Bit 7 is 0 while the button is pressed and 1 when it is released.
LDA INPT4 sets the N flag from bit 7: BMI means released, BPL means pressed. No mask is needed.
To act once per press, keep the last state in a RAM byte (FireWas): act only when the button is pressed now and was released in the previous frame, and store the current state afterwards.
Read it once per frame, in the vertical blank or the overscan, where there is time to spare, and save the result for the code that needs it.
Alternative: VBLANK bit 6 = 1 latches INPT4 and INPT5, so a short press between two reads is not lost; the latch is cleared by writing VBLANK with bit 6 = 0 and then 1 again.
techniques.example:
; FireWas: RAM byte, bit 7 = the fire state of the last frame (1 = released)
        lda INPT4          ; bit 7: 0 = pressed
        tax                ; keep it for FireWas
        bmi .Released      ; released now: nothing to do
        lda FireWas
        bpl .Held          ; it was pressed already: not a new press
        ; ---- a new press: start the jump, fire the shot... ----
.Held
.Released
        stx FireWas        ; the state for the next frame
techniques.note: After a reset the RAM is clear, so FireWas starts as 'pressed' and a button held during the start does not count as a new press.

techniques.title: Make a character jump and fall (gravity)
techniques.summary: Keep the height above the ground and a signed speed in RAM. A press on the ground gives the speed an upward value; every frame the speed is added to the height and gravity takes one off the speed, until the height reaches 0 again.
steps: RAM: Height (pixels above the ground, 0 = standing) and Speed (signed, pixels per frame: $FF = -1). Draw the sprite at GroundLine - Height.
Take off only when Height is 0 and the fire button has just been pressed (see the recipe for the fire button: read INPT4, not SWCHA).
Each frame, while in the air: Height = Height + Speed, then Speed = Speed - 1 (gravity). The jump rises, slows down, turns and falls without any table.
Landing: when Height is 0 or has gone negative (bit 7 set), set Height and Speed to 0.
A bigger take-off speed gives a higher jump (a speed of 7 and gravity 1 reach about 28 pixels); keep Height below 128 so the sign test works.
Do it once per frame in the vertical blank or the overscan, before the picture, so the kernel only draws at the new height.
techniques.example:
; Height: pixels above the ground (0 = standing). Speed: signed pixels per frame.
; JumpPressed: non-zero for the frame of a new press (from the fire-button code)
        lda Height
        bne .Air           ; already in the air
        lda JumpPressed
        beq .Done          ; standing and no press
        lda #7
        sta Speed          ; take off
.Air    lda Height
        clc
        adc Speed
        sta Height         ; Height = Height + Speed (signed)
        dec Speed          ; gravity
        lda Height
        beq .Land          ; exactly on the ground
        bpl .Done          ; still above it
.Land   lda #0             ; on the ground or below it
        sta Height
        sta Speed
.Done
techniques.note: The routine was written for this entry from the register descriptions and checked by hand, not run in an emulator.

techniques.title: Move a sprite with the joystick
techniques.summary: Read SWCHA once per frame: for player 0, bits 7 to 4 are right, left, down and up (0 = pressed). Shift each bit into the carry in turn and add to or take from the position.
steps: LDA SWCHA, then ASL once per direction: each ASL moves the next bit into the carry (7 right, 6 left, 5 down, 4 up). Carry set = not pressed.
INC or DEC the position (they do not touch the carry), then ASL again for the next direction.
Keep the position inside the screen: compare with the limits after moving (X between about 1 and 153 for an 8-pixel sprite).
The fire button is not in SWCHA: read INPT4 for it.
Player 1 uses bits 3 to 0 of the same register in the same order: shift the register four times first, or mask with AND #$0F.
techniques.example:
lda SWCHA
        asl                ; bit 7: player 0 right -> carry
        bcs .NoRight       ; 1 = not pressed
        inc PlayerX
.NoRight
        asl                ; bit 6: left
        bcs .NoLeft
        dec PlayerX
.NoLeft
        asl                ; bit 5: down
        bcs .NoDown
        dec PlayerY
.NoDown
        asl                ; bit 4: up
        bcs .NoUp
        inc PlayerY
.NoUp

techniques.title: Draw a sprite at a vertical position
techniques.summary: The sprite is drawn by the kernel: on each line compare the line with the sprite's first line, and write GRP0 with the matching row of the picture or with zero.
steps: Keep SpriteY (the first line of the sprite) and the sprite's rows in a table. In the kernel X counts the lines of the picture.
On each line: line - SpriteY. If it is 0 to height - 1 it is a row of the table, otherwise the sprite is not on this line.
Put a row of zeros after the table, and use it for the lines outside: no branch is needed to draw nothing.
Look the byte up before STA WSYNC and write GRP0 right after it, at the start of the line, so the beam has not reached the sprite yet.
The horizontal position is separate (RESP0 and HMP0); the vertical one is only this comparison.
techniques.example:
; X = line of the picture (0-191), SpriteY = first line of the sprite, 8 rows
.Line   txa
        sec
        sbc SpriteY
        cmp #8
        bcc .Inside        ; 0-7: a row of the sprite
        lda #8             ; elsewhere: the row of zeros
.Inside tay
        lda Sprite,y
        sta WSYNC
        sta GRP0           ; at the start of the line
        inx
        cpx #192
        bne .Line
; Sprite: .byte 8 rows of graphics, then .byte 0
techniques.note: The routine was written for this entry and checked by hand, not run in an emulator.

techniques.title: Random numbers
techniques.summary: An 8-bit linear feedback shift register: shift the seed right and, if a 1 fell out, XOR it with $B4. It visits all values from 1 to 255 before repeating. The seed must never be 0.
steps: Keep one RAM byte (Seed). After a reset RAM is clear, so set it to a non-zero value once (or to the frame counter when the player first presses a button, so every game differs).
Each call: LSR the seed; if the carry is set, EOR with $B4; store it. The result is the new seed and also the random number.
For a smaller range, mask it (AND #7 gives 0 to 7) or compare and subtract; avoid dividing, which is slow.
Call it once per frame or per event, not inside the kernel.
techniques.example:
Random: lda Seed           ; never 0
        lsr
        bcc .NoTap
        eor #$B4
.NoTap  sta Seed
        rts                ; A = the new number

techniques.title: Read RESET, SELECT and the difficulty switches
techniques.summary: SWCHB holds the console switches: bit 0 RESET and bit 1 SELECT (0 = pressed), bit 3 colour or black and white, bits 6 and 7 the difficulty of each player.
steps: Test a switch with BIT: LDA #mask, BIT SWCHB, and BNE when the bit is 1 (not pressed).
RESET and SELECT are momentary buttons: act on the change, not on every frame, or the game restarts again and again while it is held (keep the last state like the fire button).
The colour/B&W and difficulty switches are levers: read them when you need them.
SWBCNT must stay 0 (all inputs), which is the value after a reset.
techniques.example:
lda #%00000001     ; RESET
        bit SWCHB
        bne .NoReset       ; 1 = not pressed
        ; RESET is pressed: restart the game
.NoReset
        lda #%00000010     ; SELECT
        bit SWCHB
        bne .NoSelect
        ; SELECT is pressed: next game variation
.NoSelect

techniques.title: Start of the program: set the machine up
techniques.summary: On power-up the RAM and the TIA registers hold random values. The usual first code disables interrupts, clears decimal mode and writes zero over the whole page 0 and the stack, which also clears the TIA.
steps: SEI and CLD first: no interrupts, binary arithmetic.

X = 0, A = 0, then loop DEX / TXS / PHA until X is 0 again: the stack pointer walks down through $FF..$00 and each PHA writes a 0 there, which covers the TIA ($00-$7F, mirrored) and the RAM ($80-$FF).
After the loop the stack pointer is $FF (the top). The program counter has not been affected, so execution continues.
Then set what the game needs (colours, variables) and start the frame loop.
The reset vector ($FFFC) must point at this code.
techniques.example:
Start:  sei
        cld
        ldx #0
        txa
.Clear  dex
        txs
        pha
        bne .Clear         ; the whole page 0 and the stack are 0

techniques.title: Read a paddle
techniques.summary: A paddle is a variable resistor that charges a capacitor. Discharge it with VBLANK bit 7, then count the lines until INPT0 bit 7 becomes 1: the count is the position.
steps: Set VBLANK bit 7 for a few lines (discharge the capacitors), then clear it: they start to charge.
Count lines (WSYNC) until the paddle's INPT bit 7 reads 1: INPT0 for paddle 0, INPT1 for 1, INPT2 for 2, INPT3 for 3.
The count grows with the resistance: use it as the position. Stop at a limit (about 255) if it never reaches 1.
The fire button of a paddle is in SWCHA: bit 7 paddle 0, bit 6 paddle 1, bit 3 paddle 2, bit 2 paddle 3 (0 = pressed).
Do it every frame; the reading is noisy, so smooth it (average with the previous value).
techniques.example:
lda #$80
        sta VBLANK         ; discharge (leave it a few lines, earlier in the frame)
        lda #0
        sta VBLANK         ; charging starts
        ldx #0
.Count  sta WSYNC
        lda INPT0
        bmi .Done          ; bit 7 = 1: charged
        inx
        bne .Count
.Done   stx Paddle0        ; the position
techniques.note: The routine was written for this entry from the register descriptions, not run on hardware.
